articles.title: Let Them Sleep: Recursive Self-Pruning Memory for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
articles.summary: Agents that run for a long time have a memory problem, and it is not the one most systems optimize for. Storing every trace and retrieving the nearest neighbors works early and quietly stops working…
articles.abstract: Agents that run for a long time have a memory problem, and it is not the one most systems optimize for. Storing every trace and retrieving the nearest neighbors works early and quietly stops working later: the store fills up with failures the agent then repeats, and with facts that were true fifty turns ago. RSPM (Recursive Self-Pruning Memory) borrows the fix biology already found. At intervals the agent sleeps. It clusters its recent failures, distills each cluster into a short rule, and deletes the raw episodes it just learned from. Rules decay unless something reinforces them, and rules that recur across many contexts get promoted into general ones. We tested this on three settings with little in common: a difficulty-calibrated SWE-bench simulation, temporal consistency across 12 conversational benchmarks, and long-horizon QA on LoCoMo-10. All three improve, by 9.1, 11.9, and 7.6 points respectively. More interestingly, the two studies that instrument the store itself converge on nearly the same operating point without being tuned toward it: roughly 93% fewer retry loops and roughly 30% fewer stored entries. That hints that knowing what to forget is a general property of agent memory rather than a benchmark-specific trick.

articles.title: Small-scale neural simulation of Caenorhabditis elegans on Loihi-2 using NeuroML2Loihi
articles.summary: Neural simulation is an essential methodology for studying biological nervous systems, but it remains limited by the computational costs of repeatedly updating neural and synaptic states over many…
articles.abstract: Neural simulation is an essential methodology for studying biological nervous systems, but it remains limited by the computational costs of repeatedly updating neural and synaptic states over many timesteps. Neuromorphic hardware is a promising substrate for this class of workloads because such devices combine event-driven execution, localized memory, and spike-based communication. However, neuromorphic \textit{software} remains comparatively fragmented and difficult to integrate with the model-description standards used by the computational neuroscience community. This disconnect limits reproducible experimentation and makes direct comparison between conventional and neuromorphic simulation workflows difficult. This paper introduces ``NeuroML2Loihi'', an open-source framework for translating NeuroML model descriptions into Loihi~2-deployable Lava primitives, enabling standardized biological models to be executed on Intel's Loihi~2 neuromorphic chip. We evaluate our framework using c302-derived \textit{C. elegans} neural models across three connectome-scale configurations. Cross-platform similarity is assessed using spike-train and voltage-trace metrics, while latency, power, and energy consumption are benchmarked against the conventional reference workflow. Across the evaluated models, Loihi~2 execution enabled through NeuroML2Loihi achieves 514--1211$\times$ lower latency and a 1.8--1.9$\times$ reduction in mean wattage relative to the NEURON reference, producing substantially lower total energy consumption primarily through reduced execution time. These results demonstrate that standards-based neuromorphic neural simulation is feasible on Loihi~2 and can support meaningful comparison against established computational neuroscience workflows.

articles.title: Length-Independent Stability and $L_2$-Gain Certificates for Chains of Delayed Neural Modules
articles.summary: Networks of repeated neural modules with delayed neighbour coupling need stability guarantees for every number of modules, but delay-dependent criteria certify one network at a time and grow with its…
articles.abstract: Networks of repeated neural modules with delayed neighbour coupling need stability guarantees for every number of modules, but delay-dependent criteria certify one network at a time and grow with its size. This paper derives stability and $L_2$-gain certificates of length-independent size for open chains and rings of modules of two alternating types with slope-restricted activations. A local and a transmission delay act independently and are only bounded and continuous. A Lyapunov-Krasovskii functional with fixed integration limits and module-local variables that repeat with the module type reduces the certificate of every chain to one cell of two modules. Local conditions and a single linear matrix inequality of order 96 on this cell, or 104 for the gain, certify global asymptotic stability and a common $L_2$-gain bound for all open chains and all rings with an even number of at least four modules. Up to a margin, the stability inequality is also necessary for the repeated variables to certify every length. All uniform certificates, including certified coupling regions, are verified in exact rational arithmetic. In the numerical study, the certified coupling reaches 92% of an outer bound given by unstable members of the model class for short delays and 79% at the nominal delay bounds. For 16 modules at unit coupling strength, certificates of the same functional computed for that length alone raise the certified delay scale by 2% to 7% in four cases. A single stability problem with 1298 scalar variables thus replaces per-length certification of long chains at little cost.

articles.title: Breaking the 1/3 Barrier for Approximate Nash Equilibria in Symmetric Bimatrix Games
articles.summary: We give the first unconditional family of polynomial-time algorithms that breaks the $1/3$ approximation barrier for symmetric bimatrix games. For every fixed $δ>0$, an algorithm in this family…
articles.abstract: We give the first unconditional family of polynomial-time algorithms that breaks the $1/3$ approximation barrier for symmetric bimatrix games. For every fixed $δ>0$, an algorithm in this family computes a symmetric $(1-1/\sqrt{2}+δ)$-approximate Nash equilibrium, improving on the previous best guarantee of $(1/3+δ)$ due to Kontogiannis and Spirakis [2011].

articles.title: How Far Can an Agent Push? Trust-Safety Margins in Live Language-Based Economic Games
articles.summary: Game theory identifies when a strategic action should be accepted, but not how long a live, language-based counterpart will continue to accept it. We entered the GLEE competition in its final week…
articles.abstract: Game theory identifies when a strategic action should be accepted, but not how long a live, language-based counterpart will continue to accept it. We entered the GLEE competition in its final week with one protected agent, Milton, and four instrument agents that ran deterministic, per-game randomized trials of policy changes; Milton received changes only through pre-specified gates or registered, rollback-guarded production rules. In negotiation, learned pricing improves adjusted percentile by 0.071 (n=21,168); in bargaining, a continuation model conditioned on the rejected offer did not improve on a recency-weighted incumbent and was retired. In persuasion, a preregistered five-dose experiment (7,391 assigned games, blinded until a fixed stop) shows that recommending every unit raises sales by 0.194 of the maximum (95% CI [0.147, 0.241]) where the receiver's slack makes obedience rational (52% of the Bayesian benchmark), lowers them where it does not (-0.067), and produces a larger early-to-late purchase decline than honest recommendations (-0.123). A rule fixed before unblinding now routes Milton's dose per cell. Milton stood 11th of 460 agents in bargaining at the fixed stop; we also report the close, where the final day's pool shift moved all five agents' bargaining ratings together while their play was unchanged, and three dispatch defects were found by checking delivered behavior against the design.

articles.title: MMS Allocation for Chores with Item Disposals
articles.summary: Web platforms organize collective work, including content review and community maintenance, that imposes heterogeneous effort costs on participants. Fairly distributing these burdens while leaving as…
articles.abstract: Web platforms organize collective work, including content review and community maintenance, that imposes heterogeneous effort costs on participants. Fairly distributing these burdens while leaving as few tasks unassigned as possible is a natural objective for the design of such platforms. We study this through the maximin share (MMS) allocation problem with chore disposals under nonnegative additive costs. Our goal is to minimize the number of unassigned chores while guaranteeing every agent her MMS benchmark from the original instance. We prove that, for every instance with $n \ge 4$ agents, at most $n-3$ chore disposals suffice. We improve the bound of $2m/11+n$ disposals established by Barman et al. (2025), where $m$ is the number of chores, and eliminate the dependence on $m$. For four agents, we obtain a tight bound: one disposal always suffices, whereas known instances admit no complete MMS allocation (Ezra and Garbuz, 2026). We also prove the same result for goods: $n-3$ duplications suffice to ensure MMS.

articles.title: Strategy recovery for Mean-Payoff Games is as hard as solving them from scratch
articles.summary: Mean-Payoff Games (MPGs) form an interesting family of deterministic, infinite-duration, zero-sum, turn-based games played by two players on a finite weighted directed graph. The goal of the players…
articles.abstract: Mean-Payoff Games (MPGs) form an interesting family of deterministic, infinite-duration, zero-sum, turn-based games played by two players on a finite weighted directed graph. The goal of the players is to minimize, respectively maximize, the $\textit{limiting average}$ of the costs of the edges on an infinite path constructed by the two players. The complexity of solving MPGs is a long-standing open question. The decision problem associated with these games is known to be in $\text{NP}\cap \text{co-NP}$, and even $\text{UP}\cap \text{co-UP}$, yet the problem is not known to be in $\text{P}$. This is one of the simplest combinatorial problems with such a status. A full solution of an MPG gives the $\textit{value}$ of each vertex of the game, along with a pair of $\textit{optimal strategies}$ for the two players. (Each player has a succinct $\textit{positional}$ optimal strategy.) The problem of finding optimal strategies for the players given the values of all vertices is known as the $\textit{strategy recovery}$ problem. We describe a simple reduction from the problem of solving MPGs to the strategy recovery problem for MPGs. This shows that the strategy recovery problem for MPGs is essentially as hard as solving MPGs from scratch, i.e., without knowing the values. The reduction uses simple $\textit{game transformations}$ and simple $\textit{self-reducibility}$ and $\textit{peeling}$ arguments. This answers a question of Andersson and Miltersen. Mamino obtained a similar result for $\textit{stochastic}$ games with a limiting average objective, but his technique does not extend to deterministic games such as MPGs. We go one step further and show that finding an optimal strategy for one of the players of an MPG remains hard even if an optimal strategy of the second player, and hence all the values, are known.

articles.title: Non-Monetary Mechanisms for Stochastic Scheduling via Sampled Pairwise Externality Compensation
articles.summary: How can a shared resource be allocated without money when agents have private, stochastic demands that can be queued for a while, and may behave strategically, or even adversarially? We introduce a…
articles.abstract: How can a shared resource be allocated without money when agents have private, stochastic demands that can be queued for a while, and may behave strategically, or even adversarially? We introduce a paradigm for non-monetary online resource allocation called Sampled Pairwise Externality Compensator (SPEC). Our objective is to guarantee each agent a large fraction of its ideal utility: an individual benchmark corresponding to serving the highest-valued fraction of its demand permitted by an equal share of capacity. We seek guarantees that hold regardless of other agents' behavior, including potentially adversarial and collusive behavior. Our approach builds on the idea of pairwise externality compensation, making it computationally efficient by replacing exact calculations of future externalities with sampled estimates. The central insight is that local mixing, exploited through coupled simulations, allows these estimates to be computed efficiently while preserving robust utility guarantees. In our main technical contribution, we instantiate SPEC in a stochastic scheduling model in which agents receive jobs with private values, unserved jobs persist across periods subject to random expiration, and a single server processes at most one job per period. Our mechanism gives each agent a simple strategy that achieves the optimal worst-case fraction of ideal utility available to a fully informed planner, up to a sublinear additive loss in total utility. We also show that this fraction approaches $1$ in the long-horizon limit as the expiration probability vanishes: sufficiently persistent jobs allow each agent to secure nearly its full ideal utility. The mechanism runs in $O(n^2)$ expected amortized time per period, where $n$ is the number of agents; significantly, the expected amortized computational overhead per period is independent of the time horizon $T$.

articles.title: Improved Approximation and Tight Competition for Simple Auctions
articles.summary: We study simple auctions for one additive buyer whose values for $m$ items are independent. Write $\mathrm{REV}$ for optimal revenue, $\mathrm{SREV}$ and $\mathrm{BREV}$ for the revenues from…
articles.abstract: We study simple auctions for one additive buyer whose values for $m$ items are independent. Write $\mathrm{REV}$ for optimal revenue, $\mathrm{SREV}$ and $\mathrm{BREV}$ for the revenues from separate selling and grand bundling, and $\mathrm{BSPA}_2$ for grand-bundle second-price revenue with two independent bidders. For independent regular items, we prove $\mathrm{REV}\le\mathrm{BSPA}_2\le2\mathrm{BREV}$. This establishes tight approximation and competition guarantees for bundling under regularity and answers an open question from Beyhaghi et al. (EC 2025). For general independent items, we prove $\mathrm{REV} \le \mathrm{SREV} + \frac{π^2}{6}\mathrm{BREV} \le 2.645 \max\{\mathrm{SREV}, \mathrm{BREV}\}$. This improves the previous approximation factors of $6$ from Babaioff, Immorlica, Lucier, and Weinberg (FOCS 2014, JACM 2020) and $5.2$ from Ma and Simchi-Levi (AISTATS 2021). On the lower bound side, we construct an instance in which prices for three disjoint bundles earn more than $2.11\max\{\mathrm{SREV},\mathrm{BREV}\}$, improving the previous lower bound of $2$ from Rubinstein (ITCS 2016). We also show that exact recovery of one buyer's optimal revenue by the better of separate selling and bundling requires $Θ(\log m)$ bidders in the worst case.

articles.title: CoEvo-RSI: When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?
articles.summary: Model--harness co-evolution has emerged as a prominent paradigm for recursive self-improving (RSI) agents, jointly evolving their execution scaffolds and intrinsic capabilities. We study the…
articles.abstract: Model--harness co-evolution has emerged as a prominent paradigm for recursive self-improving (RSI) agents, jointly evolving their execution scaffolds and intrinsic capabilities. We study the persistent yet often overlooked brain--body mismatch problem in this paradigm, where an evolving harness (body) demands behaviors its model (brain) has not learned or restricts capabilities it already possesses. We introduce CoEvo-RSI, a RSI framework that advances model--harness co-evolution through agent-driven, bidirectional historical inheritance. Drawing on a shared evolutionary archive and execution feedback, a meta-agent coordinates harness development from historical designs with model checkpoint selection or merging and subsequent adaptation under the selected harness, aligning inherited capabilities with evolving execution requirements to reduce brain--body mismatch. Using only supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on its own rejection-sampled trajectories, CoEvo-RSI makes Qwen3.5-9B competitive with larger models across diverse vertical applications, including multi-agent failure attribution, role-aware text-to-SQL, and smart-home instruction following. It surpasses DeepSeek-V4-Pro on TraceElephant (+14.16 agent accuracy) and GLM-5.3 on HomeBench VM (+4.90 success rate), underscoring the need for brain--body alignment and the potential of bidirectional historical inheritance to advance agent co-evolution.

articles.title: VLA-Rolling: Fewer Denoising Steps, Better Control via Adaptive Action Reuse
articles.summary: Flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) models generate an action chunk by iteratively denoising Gaussian noise, but typically execute only a short prefix before replanning with updated…
articles.abstract: Flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) models generate an action chunk by iteratively denoising Gaussian noise, but typically execute only a short prefix before replanning with updated observations. Under this receding-horizon paradigm, the unexecuted remainder---the action tail---is discarded, and the next chunk is regenerated from fresh noise. We show that this discarded tail retains transferable denoising progress: action-tail initialization can match or outperform a native 10-step Gaussian baseline using fewer denoising steps. However, the optimal denoising budget varies substantially across samples, indicating that tail reuse should be adapted to the updated environment. Based on this observation, we introduce VLA-Rolling, a lightweight inference framework that reuses action tails through three stages: action-tail inheritance, per-action confidence estimation, and confidence-guided refinement through renoising and denoising budget allocation, while the underlying VLA remains frozen. Across π_{0.5}, SmolVLA, X-VLA, and MolmoAct2 on LIBERO, MetaWorld, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0, VLA-Rolling reduces action-chunk inference cost in all 16 model--benchmark pairs, achieving up to a 1.48times speedup, while improving success rate in 14 pairs by up to 15.08 percentage points. These results show that action tails are not merely discarded predictions, but reusable intermediate states that enable more efficient and accurate VLA inference. These results demonstrate that the action tail can support the generation of better actions with fewer denoising steps. Our project is available at https://chenbao123ww.github.io/VLA-Rolling/.

articles.title: Epi: Towards a Persistent, Self-Improving Agent for Autonomous Research
articles.summary: We present Épi, an autonomous research agent that sustains investigations across model sessions and evolves its methods through accumulated experience. Épi combines persistent research history,…
articles.abstract: We present Épi, an autonomous research agent that sustains investigations across model sessions and evolves its methods through accumulated experience. Épi combines persistent research history, hierarchical memory, branching and independent review to maintain research continuity, learn from experiments, and explore and revisit alternative approaches. Its experiments run across session boundaries, and a fixed verifier evaluates their outputs. Épi produced 120 record-setting results, comprising 20 numerical bound records across 12 families and 100 construction records across eight families. These include an approximately 84-fold narrower interval for the n-queens constant and a more than 3.6-million-fold narrower rigorous interval for the quartic Feigenbaum attractor dimension. Exact dual certificates establish that the Cohn-Elkies linear-programming bound cannot be sharp in dimensions 10 and 11. Beyond numerical improvements, Épi gives a computer-assisted proof of Tuza's conjecture for split graphs with an eight-vertex clique part and at most three triangle-active neighborhood types, with arbitrary multiplicities. We extend this research process to algorithmic coding with Épi-turbo, a lightweight configuration that develops executable solvers for tasks including vehicle routing, scheduling and production planning. On 30 FrontierOR tasks, Épi-turbo achieves a 5.4% higher total benchmark score than Codex at 64% of its model cost, using the same underlying model and reasoning effort. Épi is designed to support human understanding by connecting computational results to explicit methods and mathematical arguments that researchers can examine and build upon.

articles.title: Painting Change Map as guidance for generating painting processes
articles.summary: Digital art generation has undergone a massive paradigm shift, moving from static image synthesis to dynamic video generation that can mimic the human painting process. While existing models can…
articles.abstract: Digital art generation has undergone a massive paradigm shift, moving from static image synthesis to dynamic video generation that can mimic the human painting process. While existing models can synthesize visually stunning time-lapses of paintings being created or "unpainted," they largely treat the creative process as a black box. Current conditioning mechanisms are either too rigid, relying on static geometric cues like Canny edges or depth maps, or too holistic, utilizing simple scalar progress variables that offer no localized control. Consequently, users lack the agency to steer how a painting evolves over time. In this work, we argue that true control over the video generation of artwork requires a joint understanding of two fundamental dimensions: where an artist acts, and when those actions take place. To achieve this, we introduce the Painting Change Map, a novel spatio-temporal control mechanism that explicitly tracks normalized structural changes across a 1,000-timestep continuum, a resolution sufficient to capture fine-grained stroke-level changes while remaining computationally tractable. By mapping localized visual differences into an encoded RGB space, our representation enables fine-grained guidance for both the forward painting and reverse unpainting processes. Extensive benchmarking demonstrates the efficacy of our approach. We outperform existing control baselines and achieve competitive or superior results compared to state-of-the-art painting methods. Furthermore, under oracle conditions, our method surpasses all baselines by a significant margin. Code is available at https://github.com/Markus-Pobitzer/painting-change-map.

articles.title: PhysLDM: Latent Diffusion for High-Fidelity Deformable Simulation
articles.summary: Neural simulation of high-fidelity deformable bodies is a foundational challenge in computer graphics and physical AI. Long-horizon prediction for high-resolution 3D volumetric meshes is hard:…
articles.abstract: Neural simulation of high-fidelity deformable bodies is a foundational challenge in computer graphics and physical AI. Long-horizon prediction for high-resolution 3D volumetric meshes is hard: autoregressive methods are prone to error accumulation, while direct multi-frame prediction at native resolution is computationally prohibitive. This motivates a compact spatiotemporal latent representation, which is largely unexplored for mesh-based volumetric physics. Meanwhile, it remains unclear whether deterministic regression or generative diffusion is the more suitable predictive paradigm. To address these coupled challenges, we introduce PhysLDM, a unified latent-diffusion paradigm for one-shot deformable simulation. Its core is a holistic spatiotemporal VAE that avoids the "staircase" artifacts of standard temporal compression (e.g., video VAEs), achieving ~2.48 mm reconstruction precision on meter-scale scenes at up to 78x token compression. Based on this reliable latent space, we systematically compare regression and diffusion methods. Our experiments uncover a key modeling insight: complex deformable dynamics are often chaotic, and in this regime deterministic regression tends to produce non-physical averages, whereas diffusion better models their distribution. Accordingly, we employ a latent diffusion model that effectively learns from chaotic data to generate physically plausible trajectories. Trained purely kinematically on an Objaverse-scale dataset, a single PhysLDM generalizes zero-shot to unseen OOD datasets. Its differentiability further enables efficient solution of inverse problems and higher-order design optimization. To our knowledge, PhysLDM is the first high-fidelity spatiotemporal autoencoder and latent-diffusion paradigm for volumetric deformable dynamics, offering a scalable and robust approach to neural simulation. Project Page: https://yucrazing.github.io/physldm/

articles.title: CoworkEnv: Synthesizing Training Environments for Long-Horizon Cowork Agents
articles.summary: AI coworkers must coordinate tools, communicate across turns, and act on changing workspace state while respecting workflow constraints. Constructing training experience for these capabilities…
articles.abstract: AI coworkers must coordinate tools, communicate across turns, and act on changing workspace state while respecting workflow constraints. Constructing training experience for these capabilities requires coherent requests, service records, tool interfaces, and grading checks. We present CoworkEnv, a capability-guided framework for synthesizing executable training environments for AI coworkers. Workflow requirements guide task construction, and programmatic validation with feedback repair checks generated specifications and grading behavior. Teacher executions yield curated demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while student interactions provide rollouts and rewards for reinforcement learning (RL). Using these resources, we train compact PocketWorker models. For Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, SFT raises the mean score from 46.6 to 64.1 on Claw-Eval, including a 31.9-point gain on Multi-turn tasks. An SFT-only extension to ClawMark demonstrates applicability across coworker benchmarks. We further compare RL training dynamics across configurations that vary reward processing and credit assignment. Improving training rewards provide preliminary evidence that the constructed environments support policy optimization.

articles.title: MT Forcing: Towards Stable and Consistent Multi-Turn Image Editing with Autoregressive Diffusion
articles.summary: Multi-turn image editing aims to modify an image according to a sequence of instructions, enabling more effective interactive visual content creation for users. However, existing methods often…
articles.abstract: Multi-turn image editing aims to modify an image according to a sequence of instructions, enabling more effective interactive visual content creation for users. However, existing methods often exhibit noticeable drift after only a few editing turns, manifesting in two aspects: 1) unstable visual quality, with accumulating artifacts and degraded details; and 2) inconsistent image content, with unintended changes to preserved regions and prior edits. To address these challenges, we propose MT Forcing, a novel training paradigm for multi-turn image editing with unified multimodal models (UMMs) based on autoregressive diffusion. Specifically, we propose Single-Turn Distribution Matching Distillation (Single-Turn DMD), which supervises student self-rollouts with a teacher that applies cumulative edits to the source image in a single turn, providing visual-quality guidance without recursive error accumulation. Additionally, we introduce Teacher-Forcing Guidance, which supervises history-dependent transitions on reference trajectories during warmup and as a regularizer during distillation, encouraging cross-turn content consistency beyond what per-turn distribution matching alone can ensure. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly improves the multi-turn image editing capabilities of UMMs, yielding more stable visual quality and stronger cross-turn consistency.

articles.title: AffordanceWAM: Affordance-Aware Joint World-Action Modeling for Robot Manipulation
articles.summary: Generalizable robot manipulation requires predicting how a scene will evolve, identifying where interactions are feasible, and determining how to act. Action-labeled robot videos directly supervise…
articles.abstract: Generalizable robot manipulation requires predicting how a scene will evolve, identifying where interactions are feasible, and determining how to act. Action-labeled robot videos directly supervise control but are costly and limited in diversity, whereas egocentric human videos capture diverse interactions but lack robot actions and differ in embodiment and appearance. We introduce AffordanceWAM, an affordance-aware generative World Action Model that represents object-centric spatiotemporal affordance through Scalar Affordance and Affordance Heatmap, within the generated future World. This representation grounds visual prediction in task-relevantant objects and interaction regions for action generation, and provides shared interaction targets across human and robot videos. Built on a pretrained video diffusion Transformer, AffordanceWAM uses separately parameterized World and Action Experts, coupled through Masked Joint Self-Attention, to jointly predict future RGB observations, Scalar Affordance fields, Affordance Heatmaps, and continuous robot actions under a unified flow-matching objective. Human videos supervise all three future-World streams, whereas robot trajectories additionally provide action supervision, enabling transfer without human action labels or retargeting. Experiments on RoboCasa, CALVIN ABCrightarrowD, and real-world manipulation demonstrate consistent gains over RGB-only and robot-data-only baselines. Under fixed robot supervision, RoboCasa performance improves monotonically as affordance-annotated human video scales. These results support affordance as an effective interface for both vision-language-action learning and human-to-robot transfer.

articles.title: Think Visually Across Space and Time: Grounded Reasoning for Video Segmentation
articles.summary: Video Reasoning Segmentation (VRS) requires a model to identify an implicitly described target and predict its pixel-level mask trajectory, while resolving the spatial relations and temporal events…
articles.abstract: Video Reasoning Segmentation (VRS) requires a model to identify an implicitly described target and predict its pixel-level mask trajectory, while resolving the spatial relations and temporal events that determine the answer. Text-only Chain-of-Thought (CoT) can explain a target choice without making the underlying visual references explicit, leaving a video reference gap between linguistic inference and the evidence distributed across frames. We introduce Temporal Chain of Video Primitives (TCoVP), a spatiotemporally grounded form of Video CoT that organizes query-relevant observations into a chronological reasoning chain. Each primitive associates an entity reference with temporal support and timestamped spatial evidence, and the chain interleaves these references with language to guide reasoning about which entity is relevant, when the queried event holds, and where its evidence appears. The selected target primitives then provide box prompts and temporal support for video mask prediction. We construct TCoVP-SFT-15k and TCoVP-RL-13k to learn this representation through supervised fine-tuning and chain-aligned reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments across five VRS benchmarks and three model backbones demonstrate the strong performance of TCoVP, highlighting the effectiveness of organizing spatial and temporal evidence within the reasoning process. All models and code will be publicly released. Project page: https://victor-wjw.github.io/TCoVP/

articles.title: FineSplat: Fine Patches, Local Groups, Detailed Splats
articles.summary: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) promises instant scene reconstruction with high-quality novel-view synthesis. Yet, fine-grained geometry and appearance remain difficult to recover,…
articles.abstract: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) promises instant scene reconstruction with high-quality novel-view synthesis. Yet, fine-grained geometry and appearance remain difficult to recover, motivating us to revisit how feed-forward models represent, aggregate, and refine detailed visual information. We introduce FineSplat, a feed-forward 3DGS framework built around fine-grained image patches. Since global multi-view attention becomes prohibitively expensive at such high token resolutions, we develop a dual-grouping strategy that combines two complementary forms of locality: view-wise grouping enables efficient interaction among neighboring views, while 3D spatial grouping reconnects geometrically related tokens that may never have interacted under view-wise grouping by lifting them into the 3D scene space. We further leverage reconstruction error as direct feedback, providing an explicit rendering-based signal to recover fine-grained structures and appearance, thereby overcoming the limitations of one-pass feed-forward prediction. Finally, a compact Gaussian generation scheme preserves the benefits of fine-grained features without unnecessarily increasing the number of primitives. Together, these designs enable FineSplat to recover richer geometry and appearance while remaining efficient and compact, achieving state-of-the-art results by a substantial margin, under the same or smaller Gaussian budgets than existing methods.

articles.title: StopLoss: Teaching Agents to Predict Failure and Stop Early
articles.summary: Coding agents keep working on runs that will fail verification, and asking a frontier model to watch for this is expensive in its own right. We introduce StopLoss, a small external monitor that…
articles.abstract: Coding agents keep working on runs that will fail verification, and asking a frontier model to watch for this is expensive in its own right. We introduce StopLoss, a small external monitor that learns failure recognition from completed trajectories and their verifier outcomes. The name is inspired by the stop-loss order in finance: StopLoss ends a run early when the run is likely to fail, which saves resources. Final outcomes label earlier local windows, so a fine-tuned language model can score the most recent tool steps in a single forward pass, and a threshold calibrated on successful runs turns that score into an abort decision without changing the executor. Trained on GPT-family SWE-rebench trajectories and evaluated on SWE-bench Verified and a SWE-bench Pro subset with GPT and Claude executors, StopLoss is compared against six general-purpose judges reading identical windows. Outcome supervision lifts failure prediction from near chance to a useful signal at the first check, at one to two orders of magnitude lower cost per check than any tested judge. This translates into savings: relative to completing every task, StopLoss lowers cost per retained solve by 4.5\% on Verified while preserving 99\% of successful runs, and by up to 31\% on the costlier Pro subset, reaching 48\% with a Qwen3-8B backbone, and in all four settings its cost per retained solve is below that of every judge policy. Outcome-trained small monitors can make failure recognition cheap enough for early stopping to pay for itself.

articles.title: Policy Is Not Capability: Some Safety Benchmarks Measure Which Definition of "Unsafe" You Trained On
articles.summary: A guardrail classifier is reported as if unsafe were a property of text. It is not: it is a property of a policy, and the policy enters the model through its labels.
articles.abstract: A guardrail classifier is reported as if unsafe were a property of text. It is not: it is a property of a policy, and the policy enters the model through its labels. We exploit an accident of an industrial deployment in which the same ~53k prompts were labelled twice, under two operational definitions ("is this a request for harmful content?" and "would a moderator block this?"), and used to train ten guardrail arms sharing architecture, codebase and optimiser family, at two model scales. First, the guardrail's own training corpus already contained the benchmarks: JailbreakBench-benign is 88% and OR-Bench-hard 82% present in the training pools, two over-refusal benchmarks, the kind a guardrail reports to argue it does not over-block. Everything below is decontaminated. Second, safety benchmarks stratify sharply by how much of their score is decided by the label definition rather than by the model: with architecture and optimiser fixed, the range across the ten arms is 0.99 on HarmBench-copyright and 0.043 on WildGuard-benign, a 23x spread. Third, a benchmark score can be moved across its entire range by 0.03% of the parameters. Across these arms HarmBench-copyright spans 0-100 and OR-Bench-hard over-refusal 3.4-56.4%, and the four arms whose last supervision signal carries a given policy occupy one extreme of both (exact rank p=0.005, or 0.04-0.14 at worst), at unchanged detection capability. For a distilled student the teacher's soft labels do this even when every hard label carries the other policy, so teacher provenance is an unrecorded confound in any released checkpoint. Fourth, validation accuracy on the one split that grades all twenty arms tracks agreement with the annotator's policy (rho=+0.74), not detection capability (rho=+0.34). We argue that guardrail evaluations should report contamination, a seed floor and the definition they were graded against as first-class variables.

articles.title: World Model Interpretability: From Decoding Representations to Understanding Latent Worlds
articles.summary: Emerging Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) are moving beyond representation learning towards latent world models that support prediction, planning, and control. Yet their latent worlds…
articles.abstract: Emerging Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) are moving beyond representation learning towards latent world models that support prediction, planning, and control. Yet their latent worlds naturally lack a human-interpretable interface. In this Perspective, we argue that as JEPA latents become internal states for prediction and action, interpretability must move beyond what they encode to how latent variables interact, evolve, and causally drive prediction. To this end, we envision a four-stage research agenda, involving Ground, Structure, Verify, and Act, to guide this shift toward actionable latent-world understanding. Within our framework, existing JEPA interpretability efforts provide early evidence for Ground, while systematic analysis of latent structure, causal verification, and intervention remains largely unexplored. Overall, this Perspective aims to call for a broader latent-world interpretability agenda that shifts attention from decoding representations toward understanding, validating, and acting on latent worlds.

articles.title: Cooperation Without Shared Rewards via Reciprocal Q-Augmentation
articles.summary: General-sum games are more challenging than fully cooperative or adversarial settings because agents may deceive or exploit one another. Achieving high social welfare requires sustained cooperation,…
articles.abstract: General-sum games are more challenging than fully cooperative or adversarial settings because agents may deceive or exploit one another. Achieving high social welfare requires sustained cooperation, while a single defection can drive agents toward a welfare suboptimal Nash equilibrium. Moreover, assuming access to other agents' rewards or internal states is often unrealistic and implicitly introduces additional cooperation into the setting. To address this issue, we introduce \textit{Reciprocal Q-Augmentation} (RQA), a method that uses a latent-variable opponent model to augment the Q-function with estimates of how one's actions affects other agents. RQA allows agents to learn both cooperative and defective policies using only their own Q-function. We show that, in social dilemmas, agents that all follow the cooperative policy of RQA learn to cooperate faster and reach higher levels of cooperation than fully cooperative algorithms. Moreover, a single RQA agent that switches appropriately between its cooperative and defecting policies can induce cooperation in agents trained with standard RL algorithms, which would otherwise end up defecting. We evaluate our approach on the Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma, Iterated Traveler's Dilemma, Iterated Stag Hunt, and \texttt{CleanUp-Lite}. Our experiments show that the algorithms implementing RQA outperforms fully cooperative methods with shared rewards and enables cooperation with algorithms that otherwise fail to reach high social welfare.

articles.title: Strategic Origins of Network Structure
articles.summary: The structure and dynamics of complex networks are intimately linked. Despite immense progress in statistically characterizing these systems, a generalized mechanistic framework explaining why…
articles.abstract: The structure and dynamics of complex networks are intimately linked. Despite immense progress in statistically characterizing these systems, a generalized mechanistic framework explaining why specific mesoscale structures emerge remains elusive. Here we introduce the game-graph equilibrium, the stable rest point of a payoff-driven partner-choice dynamic, analogous to a Nash equilibrium. This reveals network structure as the fossilized record of strategic interaction. We prove analytically that two-type games have exactly four network topologies, which are their exhaustive thermodynamic phases: assortative, disassortative, and two core-peripheries. This result generalizes to $K^K$ topological classes for $K$-type interactions. Furthermore, four distinct Nash equilibria produce core-periphery topologies, yet their payoffs reveal whether the underlying dynamic is cooperative or exploitative. To recover the generating dynamics from observed networks, we develop mechanistic inference by constraining a block model to lie on a low-dimensional, game-theoretic manifold. Applied to real-world networks, the model yields interpretable quantities, distinguishes states that look identical to conventional methods, predicts network topologies it has never seen without retraining, and controls its own complexity without hand-tuned penalties. Networks such as international trade are well described by the model despite the hard constraint, suggesting that real-world systems are organized by payoff-driven partner choice. Our framework resolves a foundational ambiguity by offering a precise, mechanistic definition of communities: strategic equivalence.

articles.title: Blockchain Participation Games with Upfront Contribution Commitment
articles.summary: Blockchain participation games combine costly entry, random participation selection, and threshold success into consideration. Their retraction variants charge task-completion costs only to selected…
articles.abstract: Blockchain participation games combine costly entry, random participation selection, and threshold success into consideration. Their retraction variants charge task-completion costs only to selected contributors. We consider committee tasks whose operators reserve costly computing or communication capacity before assignment, so preparation costs are incurred even when that capacity is not selected. We characterize all pure Nash equilibria under homogeneous selection and analyze how heterogeneous selection shapes who commits. We characterize how the homogeneous minimum-outlay reward scheme supports full contribution, where every user commits, as a Nash equilibrium. Moreover, under heterogeneous selection, requiring zero registration reward can increase the minimum outlay. Finally, when full contribution is a positive-welfare social optimum, the homogeneous zero-registration-reward design attains price of stability one; and under independent Bernoulli selection, every full-contribution Nash equilibrium is also a strong equilibrium.

articles.title: Tree Plurality Veto: Voting in Few Rounds with Efficient Communication and Low Metric Distortion
articles.summary: We consider the metric distortion framework for voting, where $n$ voters and $m$ candidates are embedded in an unknown metric space. A voting rule selects a candidate using only voters' ordinal…
articles.abstract: We consider the metric distortion framework for voting, where $n$ voters and $m$ candidates are embedded in an unknown metric space. A voting rule selects a candidate using only voters' ordinal preferences, and its distortion is the worst-case ratio between the social cost of the selected candidate and the minimum social cost. We study how round complexity trades off against total communication in deterministic voting protocols with low distortion. Deterministic rules can achieve the optimal distortion of $3$ in one round by eliciting complete rankings using $Θ(nm\log m)$ bits, while a direct sequential implementation of PluralityVeto achieves the same distortion using only $O(n\log m)$ bits but requires $Θ(n)$ rounds. Our main result is TreePluralityVeto, a deterministic voting protocol that, for every $r\ge 2$, achieves distortion at most $2r-1$ using at most $r$ rounds and $O(n\log m+n s^{1/(r-1)}\log s)$ bits of total communication, where $s = \min\{n, m\}$. The protocol runs PluralityVeto on a hierarchical partition of the voters, collecting restricted rankings in parallel at each level. The branching factor controls the tradeoff between rounds and communication, and a matching-based analysis shows that each level increases the distortion bound by at most $2$.

articles.title: Spherical-Design Oracles for Zeroth-Order Optimisation: Deterministic, Variance-Free Gradient Estimation
articles.summary: In this work, we develop a zeroth-order (ZO) method that estimates the gradient with minimal bias and variance. Instead of the random directions often used in the ZO literature, we consider central…
articles.abstract: In this work, we develop a zeroth-order (ZO) method that estimates the gradient with minimal bias and variance. Instead of the random directions often used in the ZO literature, we consider central differences with directions given by a fixed spherical $t$-design, a finite point set that integrates every polynomial of degree at most $t$ exactly. The oracle is deterministic and thus does not induce any variance.We also propose a general finite difference method in the higher-order-smoothness regime and show the bias of both finite difference methods. We then show the convergence of the proposed ZO method via the input-to-state stability concept. Numerical experiments show the superiority of our proposed method over the existing random ZO methods.

articles.title: EdgeKernelBench: Unified LLM-Driven Kernel Generation for Edge Backends
articles.summary: Recent works show that LLMs can generate kernels with strong performance on server GPUs. Edge deployment presents distinct challenges because the hardware is heterogeneous, the software stacks are…
articles.abstract: Recent works show that LLMs can generate kernels with strong performance on server GPUs. Edge deployment presents distinct challenges because the hardware is heterogeneous, the software stacks are fragmented, and the resource budgets are tight. LLM kernel generation across diverse edge backends has yet to be studied systematically. We introduce EdgeKernelBench, which combines a unified IR deployment framework with a hierarchical benchmark for edge workloads. The unified IR captures reusable computation, scheduling, and memory decisions and connects to each target backend through a compiler interface. The benchmark spans progressively larger program scopes, from individual operators to compact model graphs, across representative edge application domains. We instantiate the design with TVM as a reference compiler and validate it across heterogeneous edge backends. With a single generation attempt, the best model achieves 64.5% Correct@1 but only 25.5% Fast@1.0. This gap shows that functional correctness does not consistently translate into performance gains. We therefore introduce the Layered Edge Kernel Agent (LEKA), which organizes optimization through a layered IR. On the agent evaluation subset, LEKA achieves 43.5% Fast@1.0, compared with 13.0% for direct generation and 26.1% for Claude Code. LEKA and Claude Code use the same base model and optimization budget. Together, EdgeKernelBench and LEKA support unified evaluation and layered optimization of kernels generated by LLMs across edge backends.

articles.title: Good Judgment, Bad Advice: Decision-Model Controllers Raise Agent Cost Without Improving Success
articles.summary: Agent scaffolds increasingly delegate small decisions (whether to stop, verify, or change approach) to cheaper models. We ask whether a typed decision model, Jev 1.13, consulted only at deterministic…
articles.abstract: Agent scaffolds increasingly delegate small decisions (whether to stop, verify, or change approach) to cheaper models. We ask whether a typed decision model, Jev 1.13, consulted only at deterministic decision points, makes a Claude Sonnet 5.5 terminal agent cheaper without making it worse. In a pre-specified study on Terminal-Bench 2.1, we hold one agent loop fixed and vary only the controller: none, deterministic rules, a small LLM (Claude Haiku 5.5) answering the same questions, Jev, and a placebo that samples Jev's development-phase choice frequencies at the same moments. On 21 held-out tasks (315 trials), Jev raised cost per attempt by 19% (geometric-mean ratio 1.19, 95% CI 1.02-1.36) at an identical pass rate (73.0% vs. 73.0%). Jev was cheaper than the small-LLM controller (ratio 0.81) but 22% more expensive than the placebo, and no pass-rate difference between arms was detectable. Offline, Jev ranked finish requests better than the alternatives (AUROC 0.78 vs. 0.62 for rules and 0.60 for the small LLM) but was poorly calibrated: its mean probability that a run was complete was 0.50 when 87% of those runs passed, so it asked the agent to verify work that was already correct. No controller ever chose to abandon a run. Informative decision signals did not become useful interventions; we discuss what that would require.

articles.title: HybridResearcher: Bridging the Structured-Unstructured Boundary for Deep Research Agents
articles.summary: While LLM agents are increasingly capable of gathering and synthesizing evidence from a single homogeneous source, such as structured tables or unstructured data, real-world analytical questions…
articles.abstract: While LLM agents are increasingly capable of gathering and synthesizing evidence from a single homogeneous source, such as structured tables or unstructured data, real-world analytical questions frequently span heterogeneous sources. For example, answering one enterprise question may require both a result computed over an internal database and evidence found on the web. Recent evaluations on benchmarks like HybridDeepResearch show that even frontier agents struggle when evidence must cross this boundary. While these benchmarks have exposed the limitation, methodologies to explicitly teach cross-source reasoning remain absent. To address this, we introduce HybridResearcher, a 4B agent trained to bridge evidence across the structured and unstructured boundary. To build it, we synthesize cross-source bridge trajectories by starting with validated single-source tasks-such as existing text-to-SQL or web search queries-and fabricating the missing source around a bridge entity drawn from the seed's own output. We retain a sample only when strict construction gates confirm that neither side alone suffices, ensuring the data requires true cross-source interdependence. Finally, we train on this curated dataset using supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning. Evaluated on the existing HybridDeepResearch benchmark, HybridResearcher improves over our base model, Qwen3.5-4B, by 30.0 points pass@8 and surpasses the far larger Qwen3.5-397B-A17B by 8.3 points, while also improving over its base model on established, held-out single-source benchmarks (BrowseComp and BrowseComp-Plus), demonstrating that this complex cross-source reasoning can be taught directly to small models without triggering catastrophic forgetting.

articles.title: Muse Glimmer 30B: An On-Device Agentic Model
articles.summary: We introduce Muse Glimmer, an open-source 30B parameter causal language model with perception encoder, purpose-built for autonomous agentic tasks on consumer hardware. Muse Glimmer integrates…
articles.abstract: We introduce Muse Glimmer, an open-source 30B parameter causal language model with perception encoder, purpose-built for autonomous agentic tasks on consumer hardware. Muse Glimmer integrates multi-step reasoning, reliable tool use and failure recovery into a single model that runs locally on consumer devices without requiring cloud infrastructure. The model accepts text and image inputs and produces text outputs, was trained on data from over a hundred languages, and is quantized to approximately 4-bit precision for efficient single-GPU inference. Muse Glimmer achieves state-of-the-art performance for its size class on agentic benchmarks, setting a new standard compared to the models of its size: Gemma4-31B and Qwen3.6-27B on tool use, multi-step planning, and agentic task completion. We release the model under the Apache 2.0 license to foster open-source development of capable, safe, local AI agents.

articles.title: ECHO: Efficient Causal Self-Recursion Beyond Auxiliary Multi-Token Prediction
articles.summary: Existing Multi-token prediction (MTP) methods are auxiliary by design: the multi-horizon loss mostly trains modules attached to the backbone, and each added horizon costs another module and another…
articles.abstract: Existing Multi-token prediction (MTP) methods are auxiliary by design: the multi-horizon loss mostly trains modules attached to the backbone, and each added horizon costs another module and another pass. We propose Efficient Causal Self-Recursion (ECHO), which removes both costs. The backbone's own final layer predicts every horizon, so the supervision lands on the parameters that generate the next token, and Dynamic Depth Sampling (DDS) keeps deeper horizons affordable by drawing the training depth with probabilities that decay along depth. Future prediction thus becomes part of the autoregressive objective rather than a task attached to it, and the gains follow on both sides of it. In pretraining, added depth converts into downstream accuracy where auxiliary modules saturate, concentrating on reasoning and code at half the MTP training overhead of training every depth. At inference, the pretrained model is its own drafter: it drafts beyond the depth it was trained for, and keeps its draft-target alignment on the open-ended, high-entropy generation where post-hoc drafters lose theirs. The advantage survives a doubled token budget, a repeated pretraining run, and supervised finetuning.

articles.title: Progress-Aware Distillation for Mitigating Stagnation in Small Language Model Agents
articles.summary: While LLM-based agent systems have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in reasoning and solving complex real-world tasks, they also come with substantial token consumption and inference latency,…
articles.abstract: While LLM-based agent systems have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in reasoning and solving complex real-world tasks, they also come with substantial token consumption and inference latency, limiting their practical deployment. To enhance the efficiency of agent systems, recent efforts have focused on transferring agentic capabilities from large-scale models to small language models (SLMs) via supervised fine-tuning-based distillation. Nevertheless, as interaction trajectories grow longer, involving extended reasoning-action chains and extensive environmental feedback, distilled student agents tend to experience progress stagnation: becoming trapped in unproductive loops characterized by persistent failed strategies and difficulty making meaningful progress. Our systematic analysis shows that this phenomenon consistently occurs across diverse SLMs and task domains. To address this issue, we propose Progress-Aware Distillation (ProD), which explicitly detects and penalizes stagnation in student-generated trajectories. ProD encodes the stagnation gap between student and teacher into an adaptive margin for dynamically penalizing possible stagnation. By iteratively applying this procedure, ProD enables student agents to progressively approximate teacher behavior. Extensive experiments involving 8 SLMs, ranging from 0.6B to 8B parameters, on both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, demonstrate that ProD substantially mitigates progress stagnation while enhancing both the success rates and task-completion efficiency of distilled SLM agents.

articles.title: UniAVC: Unified Audio-Video Creation via Progressive Training and Asymmetric Scheduling
articles.summary: Unified audio-video creation requires a single model capable of text-conditioned joint synthesis, bidirectional cross-modal generation, and instruction-guided editing across both modalities. Existing…
articles.abstract: Unified audio-video creation requires a single model capable of text-conditioned joint synthesis, bidirectional cross-modal generation, and instruction-guided editing across both modalities. Existing methods rely heavily on paired corpora, which are scarce for joint generation and even rarer for editing. Consequently, they are spent learning single-branch generative and editing capabilities that abundant unimodal data could readily teach, rather than on the cross-modal coupling. Furthermore, prevailing systems apply a single shared noise schedule to both modalities, neglecting two critical limitations. First, due to the significant discrepancy in information density, video requires prolonged high noise to organize spatial and motion structure, whereas the sparser audio signal can settle earlier during the synthesis process, the dynamics a uniform schedule might compromise. Second, lockstep denoising leaves asymmetric workflows, such as conditioning on one modality to synthesize or edit another, untrained. We present UniAVC, which addresses both obstacles. It first trains each branch on unimodal dataset to full generative and editing competence, and subsequently dedicates paired data to exploit cross-modal correspondence. Modality-decoupled schedulers meanwhile warp the noise schedule independently from a shared timestep, while subtasks with one clean modality directly supervise asymmetric configurations. These settings respectively enable intent-aware editing, which preserves one modality intact while enlisting it to constrain the other, and post-inference self-refinement, which regenerates only an unsatisfactory branch against an accepted one. UniAVC thus spans multiple creation tasks from a single set of weights without task-specific adapters.
